title: Raised intracranial pressure
banner: DRAFT, NOT clinically reviewed. Fictional scenario specification; never imported, published or shown to learners.
learning_objectives: Recognise early signs of raised pressure inside the skull, above all a drop in the level of consciousness, and report them urgently.
Use nursing measures that avoid raising the pressure further (positioning, neck alignment, spacing care, low stimulation, oxygenation).
Give osmotic therapy only as prescribed, and watch fluid, electrolyte, kidney and neurological status.
Understand that sedation can hide neurological signs and must be discussed with the team.

sources.use: Open RN Health Alterations 9.9: manifestations of increased ICP and the interventions box (head of bed, neck, clustering, stimulation, monitoring, sedatives)
AARC suctioning CPG: suctioning only when indicated; hyperoxygenation
FDA label: fluid and electrolyte, renal and nervous-system warnings
Brain Trauma Foundation 4th edition (monitoring sections, licensed): background only
Indexed primary guideline excerpts on osmolar gap and renal monitoring during hyperosmolar treatment.
ACS 2024 traumatic brain injury guideline, Table 10: serial neurological, pupil, hemodynamic and ICP/CPP monitoring; TBI-specific context

required_sources: Full neurocritical-care ICP/CPP appraisal and commercial-use assessment of NCS 2020 and ACS 2024; selected recommendations now linked
The unit's ICP protocol, including who sets the head-of-bed angle and what is reported
gaps: No published clinical scenario may exist until the review phase: this is a specification only.
The branching content, consequences and scoring are the author's reading of the cited sources and have had no clinical review.
NCS 2020 nonpharmacologic recommendations and ACS 2024 TBI monitoring measures now linked; no independent ventilation or drain manipulation procedure is taught.
The head-of-bed angle, blood-pressure targets and medicine choices are set by the provider and policy and are not given.

Mannitol is the prescribed fictional treatment, not a general first-line choice for every cerebral edema cause. Selected NCS 2020 monitoring statements mapped; no dose, rate, threshold or independent stop/titrate procedure.
permissions: Cited sources are paraphrased only; see the licensing register for each source's reproduction status.
setting: A fictional adult in a fictional intensive care unit two days after a bleed in the brain.

steps.info: Over the last hour the patient has become more drowsy and restless, complains of a headache and has vomited once. The monitor shows a higher blood pressure and a slower pulse than before.

observations.label: Level of consciousness
observations.value: Drowsier than at the last check

options.text: Stay with the patient, assess airway, breathing and circulation, activate urgent clinical help, and perform a focused neurological assessment including consciousness and pupils while emergency care is organised.
options.feedback: A new reduction in consciousness with headache, vomiting and changing cardiovascular findings is a warning of possible acute neurological deterioration. These findings do not diagnose raised intracranial pressure or reliably occur in a fixed sequence. Urgent patient assessment and escalation take priority.
options.consequence: The team receives a clear change from baseline and can act quickly.

options.text: Check the blood pressure again and leave the patient to rest.
options.feedback: Rechecking blood pressure alone and leaving the patient delays emergency assessment of new neurological deterioration.
options.consequence: The patient continues to deteriorate while only the pressure is followed.

options.text: Give a prescribed as-needed sedative so the patient can settle, and plan to review later.
options.feedback: Sedatives given in this situation can mask neurological symptoms; restlessness and drowsiness need assessment and reporting, not settling.
options.consequence: The change in the patient's neurological state is hidden at the moment it matters most.

steps.info: The team confirms concern about rising pressure inside the skull and asks you to continue nursing care with that in mind. The patient needs a bed bath and may need airway suction after assessment.
steps.prompt: Which approach to care is best?

observations.label: Position
observations.value: Head of bed raised by the team's order

options.text: Keep the head of the bed at the angle the provider and policy set with the neck in a neutral position, avoid sudden neck or hip bending, space the care out, keep the room quiet, and give oxygen as prescribed while monitoring pressure, rhythm, oxygenation, glucose and temperature. Assess secretion-clearance need rather than suctioning on a routine schedule, and do not delay essential airway care.
options.feedback: Interventions for managing ICP include raising the head of the bed as provider and policy direct, keeping the neck midline, avoiding sudden neck or hip flexion, avoiding clustering care, a low-stimulus environment, oxygen to prevent hypoxia and close monitoring. Suctioning an artificial airway should be clinically indicated; avoid unnecessary stimulation, but airway rescue must not be postponed. NCS 2020 supports head elevation as an adjunct with very low-certainty evidence; the team individualizes positioning according to perfusion, spinal precautions and hemodynamic tolerance. Avoid treating every pressure rise by independently increasing ventilation or adjusting an intracranial drain. Any temporary hyperventilation or CSF diversion is specialist-directed. Assess pain and essential care needs individually rather than deferring necessary care solely to reduce stimulation.
options.consequence: Measures that raise the pressure are avoided, and the patient's condition is more stable.

options.text: Do the bed bath, turning and suctioning together so that the patient is disturbed only once.
options.feedback: Combining multiple stimulating activities may raise ICP in some patients. Individualize care spacing, assess response and do not postpone necessary airway or other urgent treatment.
options.consequence: The pressure rises during the cluster of care and the patient's condition worsens.

options.text: Lay the patient flat for easier turning and washing.
options.feedback: The head-of-bed position is set by the provider and policy to help drainage from the head; lying flat is not within the nurse's own discretion.
options.consequence: The pressure rises and the patient becomes drowsier.

steps.info: The team prescribes mannitol to manage concern about elevated intracranial pressure. The patient is agitated again and a colleague suggests an extra sedative.

options.text: Give mannitol only as prescribed; monitor fluid balance, urine output, renal function, electrolytes, neurological status and ordered osmolar gap measurements. Escalate new adverse findings and discuss sedation with the team.
options.feedback: The mannitol label warns of fluid and electrolyte disturbance, kidney effects and nervous-system effects, so these are monitored; sedatives must be used cautiously because they can mask neurological signs, so the team decides. The NCS 2020 guideline favors osmolar gap over a fixed serum osmolarity threshold for toxicity monitoring during mannitol therapy, with limited evidence and no established universal cutoff. Closely follow renal function and the prescribed monitoring plan. Escalate suspected serious adverse effects promptly rather than waiting for a routine review.
options.consequence: The effect of the treatment is followed and the team keeps a reliable neurological picture.

options.text: Give the extra sedative to keep the patient quiet and note that you did so.
options.feedback: Sedation can mask neurological symptoms and must be given cautiously; the decision belongs with the prescriber after discussion.
options.consequence: The neurological examination becomes unreliable and a worsening could be missed.

options.text: Stop the osmotic medicine if the urine output rises, to protect the kidneys.
options.feedback: A rise in urine output alone does not justify stopping mannitol. Assess fluid balance and renal function, urgently escalate suspected toxicity or instability, and follow the authorised emergency or medication-management pathway.
options.consequence: Therapy is interrupted without direction and the pressure may rise again.

learning_points: A new reduction in consciousness, headache, vomiting or changing cardiovascular observations can indicate serious neurological deterioration. Assess and escalate urgently; do not rely on a fixed sequence or a single sign to diagnose raised intracranial pressure.
Position (as the provider and policy set), neutral neck, no sudden neck or hip bending, spaced-out care, a quiet room and good oxygenation help avoid pushing the pressure up.
Prescribed mannitol requires fluid balance, renal function, electrolyte and neurological monitoring; review ordered osmolar gap trends without assuming a universal toxicity cutoff.
Sedatives can hide neurological signs: discuss them with the team before giving them.
